appraisal_events.evidence: «le cas d'une vieille femme maniérée, comme Charlus qui, à force de ne voir dans son imagination qu'un fier jeune homme, croit devenir lui-même fier jeune homme, et d'autant plus qu'il devient plus maniéré et plus risible»
appraisal_events.explanation: In a generalizing aside on self-delusion in love, the narrator cites Charlus as an example of someone who imagines himself handsome and youthful while in fact becoming ever more affected and ridiculous, a mild mocking diminishment.

appraisal_events.evidence: «Morel accusait Charlus de sa tristesse [...] l'insultait de sa méfiance, à l'aide de raisonnements faux, mais extrêmement subtils, le menaçait de résolutions désespérées, au milieu desquelles persistait le souci le plus retors de l'intérêt le plus immédiat»
appraisal_events.explanation: Within an explicit comparison illustrating the strain of loving an unstable person, the narrator characterizes Morel as unjustly accusatory, insulting, and threatening toward Charlus while covertly pursuing his own self-interest.

status_effects.explanation: Cited as an example of vain self-delusion, becoming more ridiculous the more he indulges his fantasy of youthful handsomeness.
Portrayed as manipulative and self-interested, unjustly blaming, insulting, and threatening Charlus.

ambiguities: Bergotte's death is announced ('une mort qui me fit beaucoup de peine, celle de Bergotte') but the passage offers no explicit evaluative claim about him beyond the narrator's grief, so no event was scored for him.

Andrée and Françoise are mentioned only as instruments of Albertine's staged compliance and as fellow members of the deceptive 'petite bande' already captured by the accepted annotation's treatment of Albertine's lying; their involvement did not seem distinct enough to warrant separate scoring.

The Charlus/Morel material appears within an explicit narrator comparison ('Tout ceci n'est que comparaison') illustrating the difficulty of loving an unstable person, and 'le directeur' and related figures in the publishing-house analogy are hypothetical illustrative figures rather than staged scene participants, so the latter were not scored at all and the Charlus/Morel events were scored with moderate confidence given their essayistic framing.
